Bocadillo de Calamares

Spanish · Medium · Makes 4 sandwiches

Jump to Recipe Method Troubleshooting Storage
The bocadillo de calamares belongs to the northern shore of this site's sea — Madrid's Plaza Mayor, where the bars have fried squid and bread down to a system older than the tourists who queue for it: squid rings in a thin wheat crust, fried fast, piled into a crusty baguette with nothing but a smear of mayonnaise and sometimes a whisper of lemon. The Spanish coast wraps its squid in bread; the Mediterranean's west and south argue only about what else belongs inside. The honest answer: almost nothing.

Quantities live in the recipe card.

Ingredients

- **Dry the squid thoroughly.** Pat the rings dry, then let them air-dry on a towel 15 minutes while the oil heats — wet squid steams its breading off, and the flour must cling on its own. No egg wash here: the Andalusian flour-only crust depends on a dry surface. - **The bridge:** cleaned frozen squid bridges honestly (thawed and dried hard); the bread must be a real crusty baguette, and the mayonnaise should be the good Spanish kind or homemade — this sandwich has nowhere to hide its three ingredients.

Bocadillo de Calamares

Prep: 25 minutes · Cook: 15 minutes · Total: About 40 minutes · Makes 4 sandwiches

Ingredients

Ingredients

  • 600 g squid bodies and tentacles, cleaned, cut in 1 cm rings (about 550 g cut)
  • 150 g wheat flour (the Andalusian way — no egg, no crumbs, only flour) with 1 tsp salt and a grind of pepper; or half flour, half fine chickpea flour for a crisper edge
  • Neutral oil, 4 cm deep, at 190 °C
  • 1 crusty baguette (about 250 g), split lengthwise
  • 4 tbsp mayonnaise (about 60 g); lemon wedges; a pinch of smoked paprika or a dash of zhug (#99) for the dissenters

Instructions

  1. **Dust and shake.** Toss the dry rings in the seasoned flour in a bag, then shake hard in a sieve — the coating must be a breath of flour, not a jacket. Every ring separate. Checkpoint — the rings should look barely dusted, a translucent veil through which the squid shows; a thick coat fries to dough, not squid. This single step — the shake — is where the bocadillo is won or lost.
  2. **Fry fast, in small batches (90 seconds each).** Drop the rings into the 190 °C oil, a handful at a time — the oil must roar back to temperature between batches — and fry just until the edges turn deep gold, about 90 seconds. Lift, drain, salt lightly, and repeat. Checkpoint — the ring's crust should be crackle-thin and the squid within tender — this is 90 seconds' cooking, and ten more begin the road to rubber. If the oil cools between batches (the recovery test: it bubbles fiercely around a dropped ring instantly), wait; crowded, cool oil makes greasy squid.
  3. **Build at once: warm bread, mayo, squid, lemon.** The baguette split and lightly pressed open, mayonnaise in a thin film on both faces, the hot squid piled straight from the drainer — the bread's heat and the squid's must meet — and a hard squeeze of lemon over, the wedges served alongside. Checkpoint — eating test: the baguette's proper crust cracking, the squid's whisper-thin shatter giving to the sweet interior, the mayonnaise's cool richness barely containing it, lemon brightening the whole. It should taste of exactly three things — bread, squid, oil — and be complete. The paprika or zhug dissenters may proceed, one thin line, no more.

Troubleshooting

SymptomCauseFix
Crust fell off in the oilWet squid or flour too thickThe air-dry; the hard shake
Squid rubberyOver-fried or oil cooled90 seconds; small batches, full recovery
Sandwich drySkimped the mayo and lemonBoth carry — they are the sauce

Storage, Make-Ahead & Variations

- Fried squid waits for no one — 10 minutes is the ceiling; the bread and mayo can wait, the squid cannot. Cleaned squid keeps 1 day refrigerated. - Variations: the Andalusian adobo version (squid marinated in paprika-garlic first), the Catalan with alioli. The #23 whitebait cornet and this recipe are the cluster's two fried-seafood streets.

methodSteps.chefsNote: the flour-only fry is this recipe's discipline and its inheritance: a batter would cushion the squid and shift the ratios toward dough; the dusting lets the squid star, and the technique's demand — dry rings, hot oil, small batches — is what the Plaza Mayor bars rehearse by the kilo daily. When in doubt, pull early; squid carries its own heat.
